rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Where transfer is impossible, sharing takes over. Two chlorine atoms each contribute one electron to a pair both nuclei pull on — the **covalent bond**, with its single (H₂), double (CO₂) and triple (N₂) grades trading length for strength.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - Bond order = shared pairs per link (1, 2, 3) - Bond energy: single < double < triple - Bond length: single > double > triple

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Origin vs identity:** a coordinate bond looks identical to a covalent bond after formation — the arrow is history, not a property.  ·  **Diamond vs iodine:** both covalent, yet diamond melts above 3500 °C and iodine at 184 °C — network vs molecular solid; intermolecular forces set the difference.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "A coordinate bond is a covalent bond in which the shared pair of electrons is contributed by only one of the two bonded atoms."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***NH₄⁺: all four N–H bonds are equivalent*** — the donated pair becomes indistinguishable from the three original pairs; bond-length measurements confirm no special "dative" bond remains.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: covalent bond, coordinate covalent bond, properties of covalent compounds (within Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Bond of Shared Ownership Between two identical non-metal atoms there is no transfer — only **sharing**. Two chlorine atoms each bring one electron; the pair sits between both nuclei and pulls on each equally: the covalent bond. When one atom supplies **both** electrons, the link is a coordinate (dative) bond — chemically identical once formed, but with a revealing origin story.…  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Covalent bond — definition and formation - **Definition:** the bond formed by the mutual sharing of one or more electron pairs between atoms, each contributing one electron per pair. - **H₂:** two H atoms share one pair; each nucleus attracts the pair — energy minimum at 74 pm, bond energy 436 kJ mol⁻¹.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Coordinate examples: "NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺, NH₃·BF₃, O₃" — quote four. Bond energy ladder: triple > double > single. Covalent property set: "low mp, no conduct, organic-soluble, isomers, slow."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB 2024 (2m): Distinguish between ionic and covalent bonds with one example of each.** — **Ionic bond:** complete electron transfer from metal to non-metal; oppositely charged ions attract electrostatically in a lattice — **NaCl**. **Covalent bond:** mutual sharing of electron pairs between non-metal atoms — **H₂O**.…  ·  **NEB-style (3m): Define coordinate covalent bond. Describe the formation of the ammonium ion and the hydronium ion.** — A coordinate (dative) bond forms when **one atom supplies both electrons** of the shared pair: the donor must own a lone pair, the acceptor an empty orbital.…

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: When asked for properties, attach the cause: "low mp — weak intermolecular forces", "non-conducting — no free ions/electrons". Causeless lists score half.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Distinguish intramolecular (covalent, strong) from intermolecular (van der Waals, weak) forces — boiling breaks the latter, never the former. This single distinction answers most "why low mp" questions correctly.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Covalent bond = mutual sharing of electron pairs (single/double/triple; energy rises, length falls with multiplicity). Coordinate bond = shared pair from one atom (donor→acceptor): NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺, NH₃·BF₃; identical to covalent once formed.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The N≡N triple bond (945 kJ mol⁻¹) is among the strongest bonds in chemistry — the reason atmospheric nitrogen is so hard to fix industrially.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: **NEB-style (3m): Explain three properties of covalent compounds, each with its cause.** — **(a) Low melting and boiling points:** the forces between molecules are weak van der Waals/dipole attractions; melting separates molecules without touching the strong C–H or O–H bonds inside them.…

rows.text: ## 3. Scientific Definitions | Term | Scientific meaning | Value to quote | |---|---|---| | **Covalent bond** | Mutual sharing of one or more electron pairs between atoms | H₂: 436 kJ mol⁻¹, 74 pm | | **Coordinate bond** | Shared pair supplied entirely by one atom (donor → acceptor) | NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺ | | **Double bond** | Two shared pairs | O=C=O | | **Triple bond** | Three shared…  ·  ## 4. Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 Energy profile of H₂ formation - As two H atoms approach: attraction lowers potential energy; below ~74 pm, nucleus–nucleus repulsion dominates and energy climbs steeply. - The minimum (−436 kJ mol⁻¹ relative to separated atoms) is the bond energy; the internuclear distance there is the bond length.…  ·  ## 5. rows.text: Compare the bond energies and lengths of N₂, O₂ and F₂ and rationalise the order.  ·  State the limit / condition where a formula or rule stops being valid before applying it.  ·  ## 6. Common Confusions **Coordinate bond ≠ weaker bond:** after formation it is electronically identical to any covalent bond; only the bookkeeping of origin differs.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Intermolecular vs intramolecular:** low boiling points reflect weak forces *between* molecules; the covalent bonds *within* each molecule remain strong.  ·  **H⁺ never travels free in water:** it immediately coordinate-bonds to H₂O forming H₃O⁺ — writing bare H⁺(aq) is a shorthand, not a structure.  ·  ## 7. Exam Application **Verified PYQ (NEB 2024, 2m): Distinguish between ionic and covalent bonds with one example of each.** — Ionic: complete transfer (NaCl); covalent: mutual sharing (H₂O). Property contrast: mp/bp, conductivity, solubility as tabulated in section 5.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **NEB-style (3m): What is a coordinate covalent bond? Explain the formation of NH₄⁺ and H₃O⁺.** — A coordinate bond is a shared pair donated by a single atom. In NH₄⁺, nitrogen's lone pair is donated to H⁺ (empty 1s), creating a fourth N–H link; all four bonds become equivalent.…  ·  **NEB-style (2m): Why are covalent compounds generally non-conductors of electricity?** — They contain no free ions and no free electrons; the shared pairs are locked between specific nuclei. (Exceptions to mention: aqueous HCl ionises; graphite conducts via delocalised electrons.)
